claims.text: Controlled annealing of Q235 steel can promote formation of a uniform, adherent iron-oxide scale.
The annealing-induced iron-oxide scale acts as a diffusion barrier during high-temperature aggressive-salt exposure.
The protective scale retards oxidation and corrosive mass loss relative to untreated Q235 steel.
As-received Q235 steel has a patchy, non-uniform native oxide film.
As-received Q235 steel has not been homogenized or pre-oxidized.
Annealing Q235 steel at approximately 750°C in an oxidizing atmosphere can produce a continuous, adherent scale containing Fe3O4 and Fe2O3.
The proposed protective mechanism is expected to operate in oxidizing molten-salt environments at 700–900°C.
The proposed mechanism may not be effective in reducing environments or at low temperatures because oxide-growth kinetics differ.
Annealing refines the grain-boundary microstructure of Q235 steel.
Annealing stimulates uniform nucleation and growth of a dense oxide layer on Q235 steel.
The dense oxide scale impedes inward oxygen diffusion during high-temperature salt exposure.
The dense oxide scale impedes outward iron-ion flux during high-temperature salt exposure.
Untreated Q235 steel develops a less coherent oxide layer that is prone to spallation.
Spallation of the oxide layer promotes more aggressive localized dissolution.
Annealed Q235 steel will exhibit a lower net mass change than untreated Q235 steel after hot-corrosion testing.
Annealed Q235 steel will exhibit a more uniform and adherent oxide-scale morphology than untreated Q235 steel.
Annealed Q235 steel will retain its mechanical properties better than untreated Q235 steel after hot-corrosion testing.
Differences in corrosion behavior between annealed and untreated Q235 steel will be less pronounced at room temperature.
The native oxide on untreated Q235 steel offers minimal protection against high-temperature salt corrosion.
Scale continuity, density, and adhesion govern whether corrosion protection is retained.
